Hypertraces and finite injective algebras

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. New original text: public domain (CC0).

A hypertrace can remember a specified normal trace while it is approximated by finite-rank densities. Retaining that trace is the useful extra condition: a Hilbert–Schmidt vector then controls the product of left and right multiplication, and finite sums of product vectors give completely positive maps through matrix algebras. We first carry out this construction for an algebra with a faithful normal tracial state. We subsequently assemble arbitrary finite algebras from central corners and semifinite algebras from finite corners.

The spectral-projection argument is a second consequence of the same density approximation. It is developed afterwards, together with its noncommuting counterexample. Nearly tracial states are treated in a separate final module, because the finite-model construction no longer needs to obtain its chosen trace from an almost invariant projection state.

1. Conventions and exact foundations

Inner products are linear in the second variable. The symbol Tr⁡\operatorname{Tr}Tr denotes the unnormalized operator trace, and ∥x∥22=Tr⁡(x∗x)\|x\|_2^2=\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)∥x∥22​=Tr(x∗x) for Hilbert–Schmidt operators. For a tracial state τ\tauτ on MMM, write ∥x∥2,τ2=τ(x∗x)\|x\|_{2,\tau}^2=\tau(x^*x)∥x∥2,τ2​=τ(x∗x). An algebra is finite in the Murray–von Neumann sense: an isometry in it is unitary. This does not assert finite Hilbert-space dimension.

We use the definitions in Finite models of a von Neumann algebra. Semidiscreteness means a net of normal completely positive contractions S:M→Mn(C)S:M\to M_n(\mathbb C)S:M→Mn​(C) and completely positive contractions R:Mn(C)→MR:M_n(\mathbb C)\to MR:Mn​(C)→M for which RS(x)→xRS(x)\to xRS(x)→x ultraweakly, for every x∈Mx\in Mx∈M. Injectivity means completely positive extension from operator systems, with the unit value and hence the norm preserved. In particular, extending the identity of a faithfully normally represented algebra gives a ucp retraction E:B(H)→ME:B(H)\to ME:B(H)→M. The reverse implication from semidiscreteness is proved directly in Section 6 by finite matrix extension and compactness.

The faithful-trace finite-model construction below does not invoke the preceding lesson's commutant criterion. Its matrix maps and their normalization are proved explicitly in Section 5.

Three projection and trace contracts are needed for the general finite and semifinite passages, and for the final nearly tracial-state module:

  1. CT. Every finite von Neumann algebra has a positive, faithful, normal, unital, center-linear trace T:M→Z(M)T:M\to Z(M)T:M→Z(M). Thus T(ab)=T(ba)T(ab)=T(ba)T(ab)=T(ba). Every projection is an orthogonal sum of monic projections: on its central support a monic projection is one of finitely many equivalent orthogonal projections adding to the central unit.
  2. PC. Projection comparison holds. Equivalent projections in a finite algebra have equivalent complements. A finite algebra decomposes centrally into finite homogeneous type I algebras and an algebra with no nonzero abelian projection; the latter admits repeated halving of its unit into equivalent projections. On a finite homogeneous type I component, matrix units identify the algebra with Mn(Z)M_n(Z)Mn​(Z).
  3. SF. A finite orthogonal sum of finite projections is finite. In a semifinite algebra every nonzero projection contains a nonzero finite projection.

These foundations are proved in Projection comparison and normal center-valued traces: C05–C06 give comparison and finite complements, D05–D10 give the finite central decomposition, equivalent dyadic partitions and monic decomposition, NC–CT construct the normal faithful center-valued trace, and C10–C12 give the finite-sum and semifinite projection consequences. Here semifinite uses the projection convention: every nonzero projection contains a nonzero finite projection; C12 proves its equivalence to an orthogonal decomposition of the unit into finite projections. No faithful normal state on the whole algebra is assumed.

The concrete series-vector predual and its bounded strong-continuity estimate are proved in H03 of Regular-group operator foundations. Its coordinate Hilbert-space construction applies to any Hilbert space: choose a maximal orthonormal family by Zorn's lemma. H01 gives the orthogonal projection onto its closed span. A nonzero vector in the orthogonal complement could be normalized and added to the family, so maximality makes that span the whole space. Finite orthogonal truncations then identify the space unitarily with the corresponding ℓ2(I)\ell^2(I)ℓ2(I) of H00. This also covers the zero space. We use a concrete von Neumann algebra in commutant form M=S′′M=\mathcal S''M=S′′; H01 proves M′′=MM''=MM′′=M in this form.

The scalar, norming and continuous C*-calculus proofs used here are Elementary calculus for infinite products and Infinite tensor products, F01–F08. The finite threshold and spectral-step proofs S01–S06 supply the projection approximation and endpoint cuts used below, and CS01–CS06 supply the character construction. The following constructions supply convex separation, compactness, finite matrix extension, finite-rank trace estimates and the fixed spatial completion. The finite-trace realization is proved in Section 2. All closures and approximation parameters use nets. No separability assumption is imposed.

In a complex space, G(x)=g(x)−ig(ix)G(x)=g(x)-ig(ix)G(x)=g(x)−ig(ix) is a bounded complex linear functional with real part ggg. Thus this inequality also separates zero in the Banach weak topology, a contradiction. Translating proves the same separation for any point outside a closed convex set.

For the weak* topology of a dual space, a neighbourhood excluding a convex set is specified by finitely many real and imaginary parts of evaluations. Their joint map takes values in a finite-dimensional real space and sends the excluded point outside the closure of the convex image. The preceding separation argument there supplies a real linear separator; pulling it back gives a real combination of those evaluations. For hermitian functionals, each real part is evaluation at the selfadjoint part of the tested element, and each imaginary part at its imaginary selfadjoint part. Their real combination is therefore evaluation at one selfadjoint element. This is the weak* separation used below.

Products and dual balls (COMPACT). Closed scalar disks are compact by Elementary calculus for infinite products, R02. Closed subsets inherit the finite-open-cover property by adding their open complement to a cover. We now prove the arbitrary-product consequence.

A proper filter is a family of subsets closed under finite intersections and supersets, containing no empty set. Every proper filter extends to a maximal one by Zorn's lemma: the union of a chain is still proper. Such an ultrafilter contains either a set or its complement. Indeed, if adding a set would remain proper, maximality puts that set in the filter; otherwise some filter member is disjoint from it, and its complement is already in the filter.

In a compact space, the closures of the members of an ultrafilter have the finite intersection property, so they have a common point xxx. Every open neighbourhood of xxx belongs to the ultrafilter: otherwise its closed complement would belong and contain xxx, a contradiction. Conversely, an open cover without a finite subcover has complements generating a proper filter. An ultrafilter extending it cannot converge anywhere, since it contains the complement of one covering neighbourhood at every proposed limit. Thus compactness is equivalent to convergence of every ultrafilter.

For an ultrafilter on a product of nonempty compact spaces, inverse images under a coordinate projection give an ultrafilter on that coordinate. Choose one limit in each coordinate. A basic product neighbourhood imposes only finitely many coordinate conditions, whose inverse images have intersection in the original ultrafilter. It therefore converges to the chosen tuple. The product is compact. A product with an empty factor is empty and compact; the product with no factors is a singleton.

For clarity, compactness supplies subnets, not necessarily subsequences. The closures of the tails of a net in a compact space have the finite intersection property. A common point meets every neighbourhood on every tail. Use triples consisting of a neighbourhood, a tail index and a chosen later index whose net value lies in that neighbourhood. Order them by shrinking the neighbourhood and advancing both indices. They are directed: after combining two neighbourhoods, choose a hit beyond both chosen indices and both tail indices. Projection to the chosen index is order preserving and eventually beyond every original index. It defines a subnet converging to the common point.

Normal trace factorization from CT. If τ\tauτ is a normal scalar tracial state on a finite algebra, then τ=τ∘T\tau=\tau\circ Tτ=τ∘T. To verify the implication we consume from CT, take a monic projection ppp with nnn equivalent orthogonal copies summing to a central projection zzz. Traciality gives τ(p)=τ(z)/n\tau(p)=\tau(z)/nτ(p)=τ(z)/n, and center-linearity and traciality give T(p)=z/nT(p)=z/nT(p)=z/n. Consequently τ\tauτ and τ∘T\tau\circ Tτ∘T agree on monic projections. Normality and the orthogonal monic decomposition give agreement on every projection. Uniform spectral approximation then gives agreement on every selfadjoint element, and linearity on all elements. Both normality and the full monic-decomposition contract are used in this argument. The identity for singular tracial states is proved separately in Section 8.

A completely positive retraction is bimodular (MD). Here is the short dilation argument, to make this use of complete positivity explicit. For a ucp map Φ:D→B(K)\Phi:D\to B(K)Φ:D→B(K), put on D⊙KD\odot KD⊙K the positive semidefinite form

⟨∑iai⊗ξi,∑jbj⊗ηj⟩=∑i,j⟨ξi,Φ(ai∗bj)ηj⟩.\left\langle\sum_i a_i\otimes\xi_i,\sum_j b_j\otimes\eta_j\right\rangle =\sum_{i,j}\langle\xi_i,\Phi(a_i^*b_j)\eta_j\rangle.⟨i∑​ai​⊗ξi​,j∑​bj​⊗ηj​⟩=i,j∑​⟨ξi​,Φ(ai∗​bj​)ηj​⟩.

The equality for aa∗aa^*aa∗ gives the same result for a∗a^*a∗. Hence π(a)V=VΦ(a)\pi(a)V=V\Phi(a)π(a)V=VΦ(a) and V∗π(a)=Φ(a)V∗V^*\pi(a)=\Phi(a)V^*V∗π(a)=Φ(a)V∗, so Φ(ax)=Φ(a)Φ(x)\Phi(ax)=\Phi(a)\Phi(x)Φ(ax)=Φ(a)Φ(x) and Φ(xa)=Φ(x)Φ(a)\Phi(xa)=\Phi(x)\Phi(a)Φ(xa)=Φ(x)Φ(a). The same dilation construction for a completely positive map that need not be unital gives V∗V=Φ(1)V^*V=\Phi(1)V∗V=Φ(1), with bounded VVV. 2. A hypertrace with a prescribed trace

For a unital C*-algebra A⊆B(H)A\subseteq B(H)A⊆B(H), a hypertrace is a state σ\sigmaσ on B(H)B(H)B(H) for which σ(ax)=σ(xa)\sigma(ax)=\sigma(xa)σ(ax)=σ(xa), for a∈Aa\in Aa∈A, x∈B(H)x\in B(H)x∈B(H). For the converse apply invariance to xuxuxu, giving σ(ux)=σ(xu)\sigma(ux)=\sigma(xu)σ(ux)=σ(xu), and span the algebra by unitaries.

We will use the following explicit spanning formula. If x≠0x\ne0x=0, let r=∥x∥r=\|x\|r=∥x∥, a=(x+x∗)/(2r)a=(x+x^*)/(2r)a=(x+x∗)/(2r), b=(x−x∗)/(2ir)b=(x-x^*)/(2ir)b=(x−x∗)/(2ir). x=r2(u+u∗+iv+iv∗).(U)x=\frac r2(u+u^*+iv+iv^*). \tag{U}x=2r​(u+u∗+iv+iv∗).(U)

The absolute coefficient sum is 2r2r2r. The zero element needs no such decomposition.

The normal trace realization (REP). Let MMM have its concrete predual QQQ from H03, and let τ\tauτ be its faithful normal tracial state. Here normal functionals are the ultraweakly continuous functionals of that concrete predual. Complete MMM for ⟨x,y⟩=τ(x∗y)\langle x,y\rangle=\tau(x^*y)⟨x,y⟩=τ(x∗y) to obtain HHH. For x,y∈Mx,y\in Mx,y∈M, the functional a↦⟨x1,Lay1⟩=τ(x∗ay)a\mapsto\langle x1,L_a y1\rangle=\tau(x^*ay)a↦⟨x1,La​y1⟩=τ(x∗ay) belongs to QQQ. We next prove directly that its image is a von Neumann algebra. For C≥0C\ge0C≥0, let

KC={x1:x∈M, ∥x∥≤C}⊂H.K_C=\{x1:x\in M,\ \|x\|\le C\}\subset H.KC​={x1:x∈M, ∥x∥≤C}⊂H.

The Hilbert weak topology is Hausdorff, so a compact subset is closed: for a point outside it, separate that point from each compact-set point by disjoint neighbourhoods, and select finitely many of the latter to cover the compact set. 3. Finite densities retain both invariance and the chosen trace

The estimate for square roots is proved first, because it is used before any spectral projection is selected.

∥h−k∥22≤∥h2−k2∥1.\|h-k\|_2^2\leq\|h^2-k^2\|_1.∥h−k∥22​≤∥h2−k2∥1​.

p+sp+−d+=2p+kp+≥0,p−sp−−d−=2p−hp−≥0.p_+sp_+-d_+=2p_+kp_+\geq0, \qquad p_-sp_--d_-=2p_-hp_-\geq0.p+​sp+​−d+​=2p+​kp+​≥0,p−​sp−​−d−​=2p−​hp−​≥0.

c=∑iaibi∗,z=∑iai⊗JbiJ,c=\sum_i a_ib_i^*,\qquad z=\sum_i a_i\otimes Jb_iJ,c=i∑​ai​bi∗​,z=i∑​ai​⊗Jbi​J,

∑j,α⟨ξj,α,xαηj,α⟩,∑j,α∥ξj,α∥∥ηj,α∥≤∑j∥ξj∥∥ηj∥<∞.(SU)\sum_{j,\alpha}\langle\xi_{j,\alpha},x_\alpha\eta_{j,\alpha}\rangle, \qquad \sum_{j,\alpha}\|\xi_{j,\alpha}\|\|\eta_{j,\alpha}\| \le\sum_j\|\xi_j\|\|\eta_j\|<\infty. \tag{SU}j,α∑​⟨ξj,α​,xα​ηj,α​⟩,j,α∑​∥ξj,α​∥∥ηj,α​∥≤j∑​∥ξj​∥∥ηj​∥<∞.(SU)

At every matrix level, vector tests of a positive image matrix are normal functionals of its finitely many entries, so their nonnegativity passes to the limit; thus Ψ\PsiΨ is completely positive. Lemma 6.1. Every corner of an injective von Neumann algebra is injective.

Proof. Let Φ:S→eMe\Phi:S\to eMeΦ:S→eMe be a completely positive map on an operator system in a unital C*-algebra DDD. Include its values in MMM and extend by injectivity to a completely positive map Ψ:D→M\Psi:D\to MΨ:D→M. Compression a↦eΨ(a)ea\mapsto e\Psi(a)ea↦eΨ(a)e is completely positive at every matrix level, agrees with Φ\PhiΦ, and has the same unit value. It is the required extension into eMeeMeeMe. The two-by-two unit-value norm formula in FEXT gives preservation of the norm. For e=0e=0e=0 the zero extension suffices. □\square□

Lemma 6.2. Suppose projections ei∈Me_i\in Mei​∈M increase strongly to one and every eiMeie_iMe_iei​Mei​ is semidiscrete. Then MMM is semidiscrete.

Proof. The maps Ci(x)=eixeiC_i(x)=e_ixe_iCi​(x)=ei​xei​ are cpc: at each matrix level they are compression by a diagonal orthogonal projection, which preserves positivity and has norm at most one. They are normal because composing a series-vector functional with CiC_iCi​ replaces each pair (ξj,ηj)(\xi_j,\eta_j)(ξj​,ηj​) by (eiξj,eiηj)(e_i\xi_j,e_i\eta_j)(ei​ξj​,ei​ηj​), whose sum of norm products is no larger. For fixed xxx,

∥(eixei−x)ξ∥≤∥x∥∥(ei−1)ξ∥+∥(ei−1)xξ∥⟶0.\|(e_ixe_i-x)\xi\| \le\|x\|\|(e_i-1)\xi\|+\|(e_i-1)x\xi\|\longrightarrow0.∥(ei​xei​−x)ξ∥≤∥x∥∥(ei​−1)ξ∥+∥(ei​−1)xξ∥⟶0.

Apply this also to x∗x^*x∗. Thus the compressions converge strongly* to xxx, and their uniform norm bound gives ultraweak convergence by the series-vector estimate of H03. Given finitely many operators xxx, normal functionals fff, and a tolerance, choose one index iii that meets all compression errors below half the tolerance; directedness permits this simultaneous choice. On the semidiscrete corner choose normal cpc S:eiMei→MnS:e_iMe_i\to M_nS:ei​Mei​→Mn​ and cpc R:Mn→eiMeiR:M_n\to e_iMe_iR:Mn​→ei​Mei​ meeting the remaining tests for Ci(x)C_i(x)Ci​(x) and fff restricted to the corner. The normal cpc incoming map SCiSC_iSCi​, and the outgoing map given by RRR followed by the cpc corner inclusion, meet the original tests by the triangle inequality. Directing over every finite test list and positive tolerance produces the pointwise ultraweak net. Zero corners and the zero algebra simply give zero maps until nonzero tests require a larger corner. □\square□

Corollary 6.3. Every semifinite injective von Neumann algebra is semidiscrete, without factor or countability assumptions.

Proof. By SF every nonzero projection contains a nonzero finite projection. A maximal orthogonal family (pα)(p_\alpha)(pα​) of nonzero finite projections must therefore have supremum one: a nonzero complement would provide a further such projection. For finite GGG, its sum eG=∑α∈Gpαe_G=\sum_{\alpha\in G}p_\alphaeG​=∑α∈G​pα​ is finite by SF. Thus eGMeGe_GMe_GeG​MeG​ is a finite algebra, injective by Lemma 6.1, and semidiscrete by Theorem 5.3. The finite-partial-sum net increases strongly to one; apply Lemma 6.2. The zero algebra is covered directly by zero matrix maps. No projection is assumed to have finite Hilbert-space rank, and no maximal family is assumed countable. □\square□

This proves existence of a finite list and γ>0\gamma>0γ>0. The compactness argument uses the norm-averaging identity ALL, which applies to singular as well as normal tracial states. □\square□

9. Exercises with solutions

Exercise 1. Let h,k≥0h,k\geq0h,k≥0 be finite matrices. Why is it legitimate to multiply a positive matrix inequality by another positive matrix and take the trace, even when the matrices do not commute? Apply this observation to the proof of Lemma 1.1.

Solution. If A≥BA\geq BA≥B and C≥0C\geq0C≥0, then C1/2(A−B)C1/2≥0C^{1/2}(A-B)C^{1/2}\geq0C1/2(A−B)C1/2≥0. Its trace is Tr⁡((A−B)C)\operatorname{Tr}((A-B)C)Tr((A−B)C) by cyclicity, hence is nonnegative. In Lemma 1.1 use A=p+sp+A=p_+sp_+A=p+​sp+​, B=d+B=d_+B=d+​, C=d+C=d_+C=d+​. This gives Tr⁡(p+sp+d+)≥Tr⁡(d+2)\operatorname{Tr}(p_+sp_+d_+)\geq\operatorname{Tr}(d_+^2)Tr(p+​sp+​d+​)≥Tr(d+2​). The negative support gives Tr⁡(p−sp−d−)≥Tr⁡(d−2)\operatorname{Tr}(p_-sp_-d_-)\geq\operatorname{Tr}(d_-^2)Tr(p−​sp−​d−​)≥Tr(d−2​). Add and use orthogonality of the supports to get Tr⁡(s∣d∣)≥Tr⁡(d2)\operatorname{Tr}(s|d|)\geq\operatorname{Tr}(d^2)Tr(s∣d∣)≥Tr(d2). No assertion that the products themselves are ordered or selfadjoint is made.

Exercise 2. Prove the scalar threshold identity

∫0∞∣1s>t−1v>t∣2 dt=∣s2−v2∣(s,v≥0).\int_0^\infty|1_{s>\sqrt t}-1_{v>\sqrt t}|^2\,dt =|s^2-v^2|\qquad(s,v\geq0).∫0∞​∣1s>t​​−1v>t​​∣2dt=∣s2−v2∣(s,v≥0).

Explain why the square-root threshold matters for Theorem 2.1.

Solution. If s≥vs\geq vs≥v, the indicators differ exactly for v2<t<s2v^2<t<s^2v2<t<s2, except for endpoints; their squared difference is one there. Integration gives s2−v2s^2-v^2s2−v2. Exchanging s,vs,vs,v proves the other case, including equality and zero values. Applying the same threshold to each eigenvalue gives ∫Tr⁡(Pt(h))dt=Tr⁡(h2)\int\operatorname{Tr}(P_t(h))dt=\operatorname{Tr}(h^2)∫Tr(Pt​(h))dt=Tr(h2). When hhh is the square root of a state density this is one, which is the normalization used in the threshold contradiction for Theorem 2.1. Using the threshold ttt instead of t\sqrt tt​ would integrate rank to Tr⁡(h)\operatorname{Tr}(h)Tr(h), and that quantity need not be one.

Exercise 3. For mmm prescribed unitaries, verify explicitly that the choice δ=ε4/(16m)\delta=\varepsilon^4/(16m)δ=ε4/(16m) in Theorem 2.1 gives a nonzero projection satisfying all the required commutator bounds.

Solution. For m≥1m\geq1m≥1, substitution gives 2mδ=ε2/22\sqrt{m\delta}=\varepsilon^2/22mδ​=ε2/2. The squared-error integral in Theorem 2.1 is strictly below this number, and the rank integral is one. If the sum of squared errors were at least ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 times rank at every nonzero threshold outside a null set, its integral would be at least ε2\varepsilon^2ε2. This contradicts the strict upper bound. Therefore a threshold with positive finite rank rrr has the sum strictly below ε2r\varepsilon^2rε2r. Every summand is nonnegative and hence strictly below that bound; square roots and ∥p−uj∗puj∥2=∥[p,uj]∥2\|p-u_j^*pu_j\|_2=\|[p,u_j]\|_2∥p−uj∗​puj​∥2​=∥[p,uj​]∥2​ give all required inequalities. For m=0m=0m=0 the displayed choice involving division is not used: a rank-one projection suffices.

Exercise 4. For projections p,qp,qp,q of the same finite rank rrr, prove ∥p−q∥1≤2r∥p−q∥2\|p-q\|_1\leq2\sqrt r\|p-q\|_2∥p−q∥1​≤2r​∥p−q∥2​. Deduce the state estimate preceding Section 4.

Solution. Expand p−q=p(p−q)+(p−q)qp-q=p(p-q)+(p-q)qp−q=p(p−q)+(p−q)q. The finite-rank Hölder bound (F2) and ∥p∥2=∥q∥2=r\|p\|_2=\|q\|_2=\sqrt r∥p∥2​=∥q∥2​=r​ give ∥p−q∥1≤2r∥p−q∥2\|p-q\|_1\leq2\sqrt r\|p-q\|_2∥p−q∥1​≤2r​∥p−q∥2​. This remains true for r=0r=0r=0, when both projections vanish. To discuss a projection state take r>0r>0r>0. Cyclicity gives ρp(x)=Tr⁡(px)/r\rho_p(x)=\operatorname{Tr}(px)/rρp​(x)=Tr(px)/r, and the conjugated state has density u∗pu/ru^*pu/ru∗pu/r. The finite-rank norm formula (F1) gives the exact norm ∥p−u∗pu∥1/r\|p-u^*pu\|_1/r∥p−u∗pu∥1​/r; multiplying the commutator by a unitary gives ∥p−u∗pu∥2=∥[p,u]∥2\|p-u^*pu\|_2=\|[p,u]\|_2∥p−u∗pu∥2​=∥[p,u]∥2​. Combining the identities yields (P), the state estimate preceding Section 4.

Exercise 5. Let A=M2(C)⊕M3(C)A=M_2(\mathbb C)\oplus M_3(\mathbb C)A=M2​(C)⊕M3​(C). Compute its center-valued trace. Give c∈Ac\in Ac∈A for which a tracial state can satisfy ρ(c)=0\rho(c)=0ρ(c)=0 although ∥T(c)∥=1\|T(c)\|=1∥T(c)∥=1. Explain the role of central localization.

Solution. With normalized numerical matrix traces, T(x⊕y)=tr⁡2(x)12⊕tr⁡3(y)13T(x\oplus y)=\operatorname{tr}_2(x)1_2\oplus\operatorname{tr}_3(y)1_3T(x⊕y)=tr2​(x)12​⊕tr3​(y)13​. For c=12⊕(−13)c=1_2\oplus(-1_3)c=12​⊕(−13​), the tracial state ρ=(tr⁡2+tr⁡3)/2\rho=(\operatorname{tr}_2+\operatorname{tr}_3)/2ρ=(tr2​+tr3​)/2 takes value zero, but T(c)=cT(c)=cT(c)=c has norm one. The central projection 12⊕01_2\oplus012​⊕0 cuts away the cancelling summand. On that corner T(c)T(c)T(c) is the unit, so every corner state takes value one. Thus one average over the whole center can miss the norm. Theorem 4.2 detects the same phenomenon by allowing every normal central state. The state supported on the first summand is among its tests; composing it with the center-valued trace gives the normal tracial state to which the fixed spatial bound SC applies.

Exercise 6. Let a unital -algebra DDD act on HHH by μ\muμ, with cyclic unit vector ξ\xiξ. Suppose z↦⟨ξ,μ(z)ξ⟩z\mapsto\langle\xi,\mu(z)\xi\ranglez↦⟨ξ,μ(z)ξ⟩ extends to a state on a C-completion CCC of DDD. Prove that μ\muμ extends to a contractive representation of CCC.

Solution. Let Ω\OmegaΩ be the extended state, and use the complete GNS construction in Section 1, restricting its dense quotient vectors to DDD. The map [z]↦μ(z)ξ[z]\mapsto\mu(z)\xi[z]↦μ(z)ξ is well defined, because the squared norm of its image is exactly Ω(z∗z)\Omega(z^*z)Ω(z∗z); polarization also preserves inner products. Its range is dense by the assumed cyclicity of ξ\xiξ, so completion gives a unitary from the GNS space onto HHH. The GNS representation of CCC restricts on the dense algebraic subspace to left multiplication. For w,z∈Dw,z\in Dw,z∈D, the unitary sends [wz][wz][wz] to μ(w)μ(z)ξ\mu(w)\mu(z)\xiμ(w)μ(z)ξ, so it intertwines this restriction with μ(w)\mu(w)μ(w). Transporting the bounded GNS representation of CCC gives the required extension; a -representation of a C-algebra is contractive. Theorem 5.1 constructs its matrix maps directly, so it does not require this intermediate cyclic transport.

Exercise 7. For an arbitrary set III, give explicit normal cpc matrix factorizations witnessing semidiscreteness of ℓ∞(I)\ell^\infty(I)ℓ∞(I). Why can III uncountable prevent a faithful normal state?

Solution. For a nonempty finite G⊆IG\subseteq IG⊆I, let SG(x)=diag⁡(x(i))i∈G∈M∣G∣S_G(x)=\operatorname{diag}(x(i))_{i\in G}\in M_{|G|}SG​(x)=diag(x(i))i∈G​∈M∣G∣​. Let RGR_GRG​ take the diagonal entries of a matrix to the corresponding coordinates of ℓ∞(I)\ell^\infty(I)ℓ∞(I), putting zero elsewhere. Coordinate evaluation and diagonal compression are completely positive contractions, and SGS_GSG​ is normal. Their composite is eGxe_GxeG​x. The normal-functional coefficients are exactly ℓ1(I)\ell^1(I)ℓ1(I). Indeed, expand an H03 series-vector functional on the diagonal representation on ℓ2(I)\ell^2(I)ℓ2(I): its coefficient at iii is ci=∑jξj(i)‾ηj(i)c_i=\sum_j\overline{\xi_j(i)}\eta_j(i)ci​=∑j​ξj​(i)​ηj​(i). Cauchy–Schwarz gives ∑i∣ci∣≤∑j∥ξj∥∥ηj∥<∞\sum_i|c_i|\le\sum_j\|\xi_j\|\|\eta_j\|<\infty∑i​∣ci​∣≤∑j​∥ξj​∥∥ηj​∥<∞, so absolute summation yields f(x)=∑icix(i)f(x)=\sum_i c_ix(i)f(x)=∑i​ci​x(i). Conversely, for any summable family (ci)(c_i)(ci​), put ξ(i)=∣ci∣\xi(i)=\sqrt{|c_i|}ξ(i)=∣ci​∣​ and η(i)=ci/∣ci∣\eta(i)=c_i/\sqrt{|c_i|}η(i)=ci​/∣ci​∣​, both zero when ci=0c_i=0ci​=0. These are square-summable vectors and ⟨ξ,xη⟩=∑icix(i)\langle\xi,x\eta\rangle=\sum_i c_ix(i)⟨ξ,xη⟩=∑i​ci​x(i), hence a normal functional. The tail of a summable family outside finite GGG tends to zero; consequently eGx→xe_Gx\to xeG​x→x ultraweakly. For I=∅I=\varnothingI=∅ the algebra is zero and zero maps through M1M_1M1​ suffice. A normal state has nonnegative summable weights of total one. For each positive integer mmm, only finitely many weights can be at least 1/m1/m1/m; the union of those finite sets contains every positive weight and is countable. If III is uncountable, some nonzero coordinate projection has weight zero, so the state is not faithful.

Exercise 8. Suppose MMM is semifinite and injective. In the proof of Corollary 6.3, explain why finite projections refer to Murray–von Neumann finiteness, not finite Hilbert-space rank. Show how a completely positive finite model on a corner becomes one on MMM.

Solution. Murray–von Neumann finiteness means eee has no equivalent proper subprojection inside MMM. It makes eMeeMeeMe a finite von Neumann algebra, while the space eHeHeH can still be infinite-dimensional. Given normal cpc S:eMe→MnS:eMe\to M_nS:eMe→Mn​ and cpc R:Mn→eMeR:M_n\to eMeR:Mn​→eMe, the incoming map on MMM is x↦S(exe)x\mapsto S(exe)x↦S(exe); the outgoing map is RRR followed by the corner inclusion. Compression is normal and cpc, and the inclusion is cpc, so these are the required kinds of maps. For increasing corners, bounded strong* convergence gives exe→xexe\to xexe→x ultraweakly. On any finite collection of operator and normal-functional tests choose the corner to make the compression error small, then choose its finite model to make the model error small. Their sum bounds the error on MMM, which is precisely the net construction in Lemma 6.2.

Reading

  • Claire Anantharaman and Sorin Popa, An introduction to II1 factors, author-hosted draft. Theorem 7.3.7, printed pp.109–110, supplies the sign-support Powers–Størmer method; Proposition 10.2.5, Lemma 10.2.6 and the whole proof of Theorem 10.2.9, pp.163–165, supply the prescribed-trace convexity route. Proposition 10.3.3 and Theorem 10.3.4, pp.167–169, supply the spectral-overlap calculation. The complete Theorem 13.4.2 proof, pp.232–233, explicitly factors finite-product-vector coefficients through matrices. Lemma 13.1.11, p.219, supplies the standard marginal cutoff. Theorem 5.1 gives a complete one-marginal specialization with ultraweak tests, without importing general bimodule machinery.
  • William B. Arveson, Subalgebras of C*-algebras, Acta Mathematica 123 (1969), 141–224. Theorem 1.1.1 gives the dilation construction used in MD. Theorem 1.2.3 gives the general extension theorem by a separation argument; the finite-target scalar construction FEXT here is instead the method described in Peterson, Lemma 8.4.5.
  • Jesse Peterson, Notes on operator algebras, dated April 27, 2020. Proposition 6.4.12 supplies the elementary finite-trace commutant proof. Lemma 8.4.5, p.147, describes finite-target extension through a scalar functional; FEXT writes out this method while preserving every matrix-unit value at one. Chapters 5–6 develop the comparison, homogeneous type I, halving, monic-decomposition and center-trace theorems used in CT, PC and SF.
